units.la: I.
units.tr: I.

units.la: VANDOQVIDEM Adversarii nostri religionis suae proram & puppim constituunt in Missa sacrificio: baud iniquè facere videntur homines veritatis amantes, si qualenam illud sit, & quid de eo credere aut sentire debeant, sape apud se cogitent, diligenterq; expendant. Vt autem juxta sapiens Epicteti dictum, Ἀρχὴ παιδεύσεως ἡ τῶν ὀνομάτων ἐπίσκεψις, Principium doctrinae est consideratio nominum: ita Missae quoq; nomen ante omnia imprasentiarum considerare juvat. Quo cognito, ipsam disputationis hujusce arcem, divinâ adjuvante Clementiâ aggrediemur.
units.tr: Since our adversaries make the Mass the prow and stern of their religion, it is not unreasonable for lovers of the truth to think often about what it is, and what they ought to believe and think about it, and to weigh it carefully. As the wise saying of Epictetus has it, "The beginning of education is the examination of names" [Ἀρχὴ παιδεύσεως ἡ τῶν ὀνομάτων ἐπίσκεψις], so it is helpful to consider first the name of the Mass. Once that is known, by the gracious help of God we shall attack the citadel of this dispute itself.

units.la: II.
units.tr: II.

units.la: Missae nomine probati auctores Syri, Graeci, Latini, qui a Christo in carne nato per annos trecentos & amplius scripserunt, non sunt usi. Unde Syrus, novi Testamenti interpres, vocem Graecam εὐχαριστία retinet. Et Iustinus, Ignatius, Irenaeus, Tertullianus, Origenes, Cyprianus, alii; quorum certa scripta ad nos pervenerunt, intra illud tempus, quum vivèrent, multa de sacra Coena disseruerunt: at horum ne unus quidem istius appellationis meminit. Quod notandum contra Card. Baronium; qui in annalibus suis asserere non dubitat, Missae nomen a Iacobo, τοῦ Ἀδελφοθέου, Hierosolymitanis: a Petro verò & Paulo Romanis traditum; ac proinde antiquissimum esse.
units.tr: The approved authors who wrote in Syriac, Greek and Latin during the three hundred and more years after Christ was born in the flesh did not use the name Mass. So the Syrian, translator of the New Testament, keeps the Greek word "thanksgiving" [εὐχαριστία]. Justin, Ignatius, Irenaeus, Tertullian, Origen, Cyprian and others, whose genuine writings have come down to us, discussed the holy Supper at length in that period while they lived, yet not one of them mentions this name. This must be noted against Cardinal Baronius, who does not hesitate to assert in his Annals that the name Mass was handed down by James, "the brother of God" [τοῦ Ἀδελφοθέου], to the Jerusalemites, and by Peter and Paul to the Romans, and that it is therefore very ancient.

units.la: III.
units.tr: III.

units.la: Iam verò Missae nomen ortum habere ab Hebraeis, vel Chaldaeis, commentum est hominum, neq; Hebraeas, neq; Chaldaeas litteras intelligentium, aut certè judicii prorsus nullius. Legitur sanè in Graecorum monumentis vox Μίσα: sed auctorum media aetatis; qui ante annos praeter propter sexcentos de re militari scripserunt: verum pro precibus vespertinis, aut matutinis sumtâ voce, non pro sacra Eucharistia.
units.tr: That the name Mass arose among the Hebrews or the Chaldeans is an invention of men who understand neither Hebrew nor Chaldean letters, or at least are wholly without judgment. It is true that the word "Missa" [Μίσα] is found in Greek documents, but in writers of the middle ages, who wrote about military affairs some six hundred years ago; and there it means the evening or morning prayers, not the holy Eucharist.

units.la: IV.
units.tr: IV.

units.la: Originem igitur Latinam habet vox Missa, aliis omnibus linguis, nisi quæ a Latina acceperunt, incognita. Sunt qui putent primò Missas, cùm Missa missorum, dictum fuisse, proprièq; eam vocem oblationes significare: quæ vel afferebantur, vel mittebantur, & sacræ mensæ imponebantur. Verum enimverò nos, unâcum gloriosæ memoriæ viro, Isaaco Casaubono, affirmare non veremur, Missam, vel, quod idem est, Missionem esse ἄφεσιν: quam vocem Græcis olim in dimittenda concione fuisse usitatam, ex Plutarcho & aliis scriptoribus constat: quo modo in judiciis & exsequiis Romanorum, quum præco & præfica clamabant Ilicet, quasi Ire licet, judicibus, & iis; qui exsequias peragebant, abeundi facta potestas intelligebatur. Et apud Græcos quidem ejusmodi ἄφεσις, vel Missa, vel Missio fuit duntaxat una, quum scilicet finitâ concione præconis voce clamabatur, λαῶν ἄφεσις, in liturgia verò veteres Christianorum fuit duplex: prior; quum finitis lectionibus sacræ scripturæ, & precibus illis; quibus poterant interesse catechumeni, energumeni, & alii non initiati, voce diaconi jubebantur exire, quibus sacram liturgiam spectare fas non erat: posterior; quum sacris peractis, & Eucharistiæ celebratione finitâ, post ἐυχὴν ἀπολυτικὴν, a diacono pronunciatam populo discedendi fiebat potestas: quod in liturgia Chrysostomi intelligitur illis verbis ὁ ἱερεὺς ποιεῖ ἀπόλυσιν, sacerdos facit Missam, seu Missionem, hoc est, dimittit populum: adeò ut ἀπόλυσις sit ἄφεσις, Missa seu Missio, sumto verbo e Simeonis cantico, Νῦν ἀπολύεις τὸν δοῦλόν σου δέσποτα[?]; quæ ibidem recitantur, &c. Ex quibus apparet, liturgia Veterum duas fuisse partes, quæ propter totidem missiones dictæ sunt Missæ: prior videlicet catechumenorum, ut dictum, & ex can. 84. concilii Carthagin. quarti liquet: posterior verò fidelium; quæ κατ' ἐξοχὴν ut sola diceretur Missa tandem obtinuit: circa finem nimirum, ut videtur, seculi tertii vel paulò ante, &c.
units.tr: The word Mass therefore has a Latin origin, and is unknown in all other languages except those which received it from Latin. Some think that at first it was called "Missa" from "missa missorum", and that the word properly signified the offerings which were either brought forward or sent and placed on the holy table. But we, together with the man of glorious memory, Isaac Casaubon, do not hesitate to affirm that Mass, or what is the same thing, Missio, means dismissal [ἄφεσις]. From Plutarch and other writers it is clear that the Greeks once used this word when dismissing an assembly. Thus in Roman trials and funerals, when the herald and the mourning woman cried "Ilicet", that is, "you may go", to the judges and to those who conducted the funeral, the permission to depart was understood. Among the Greeks this dismissal, or Mass or Missio, took only one form, when the assembly was finished and the herald's voice cried "the dismissal of the people" [λαῶν ἄφεσις]. In the liturgy of the early Christians, however, there was a double dismissal. The first came when the readings of Holy Scripture and those prayers were finished, at which the catechumens, the energumens and the other uninitiated, to whom it was not lawful to watch the holy liturgy, were bidden by the deacon's voice to leave. The second came when the sacred rites were done and the celebration of the Eucharist was finished: after the dismissal prayer [ἐυχὴν ἀπολυτικὴν], pronounced by the deacon, the people were given leave to depart. This is understood in the liturgy of Chrysostom from the words "the priest makes the dismissal" [ὁ ἱερεὺς ποιεῖ ἀπόλυσιν], that is, "the priest makes the Mass, or Missio, that is, dismisses the people". So dismissal [ἀπόλυσις] is the same as permission [ἄφεσις], Mass or Missio, the word being taken from the canticle of Simeon, "Now you let your servant depart, Master" [Νῦν ἀπολύεις τὸν δοῦλόν σου δέσποτα], which is recited there, etc. From these things it appears that the liturgy of the ancients had two parts, and for that reason each was called a Mass, that is, a dismissal: the first, of the catechumens, as has been said, and as is clear from canon 84 of the Fourth Council of Carthage; the second, of the faithful, which at last came to be called simply "the Mass" [κατ' ἐξοχὴν], probably about the end of the third century or a little before, etc.

units.la: V.
units.tr: V.

units.la: Posteriùs temporibus, vox Missa alios etiam sensus est sortita ab iis, qui primi in scribendo frequentârunt. Hinc Ambrosius Missam facere dixit pro celebrare liturgiam ad sacram Eucharistiam: quod verbum offero, & alia; quæ sequuntur, satis arguunt. Et in precationibus ejus præparantibus ad Missam, Missa illi est Eucharistia: quod declarat totus illarum contextus. Alibi, apud eundem & alios, Missarum celebratio celebratio latinis patet: quod facile cuivis est observare. Quandoq; legitur Missam audire pro audire liturgiam & communionem: sed alio sensu; quàm quo hodie locutio illa usurpatur ab iis; quibus Missa communio non est, sed ἀχρόαμα duntaxat et spectaculum inane. Et illo quidem sensu extat apud Gratianum ex Agathensi concilio, & apud eundem Ambr. Sermo. 34. De quadr. Locutisic sunt & Græci, æquales Ambrosio, aut etiam priores. Eusebius enim εὐχαριστίας ἐπιτυγχάνειν Missam audire de eo dixit, quem narrat communicasse.
units.tr: In later times the word Mass acquired other meanings from those who first used it frequently in writing. Thus Ambrose said that he "made Mass" for "celebrated the liturgy" of the holy Eucharist: "the words 'I offer' and what follows sufficiently prove this". And in his prayers preparing for the Mass, Mass means for him the Eucharist: "the whole context of those prayers makes this clear". Elsewhere, in Ambrose and others, "celebration of Masses" is plainly a Latin phrase, as anyone can easily see. Sometimes we read "to hear Mass" for "to attend the liturgy and communion". But this is in a different sense from that in which the phrase is now used by those for whom Mass is not communion but merely a show [ἀχρόαμα] and an empty spectacle. In that sense it occurs in Gratian, from the Council of Agde, and in Ambrose's Sermon 34 On Lent. The Greeks too, contemporary with Ambrose or even earlier, spoke in the same way: Eusebius said of a man whom he reports as having communicated that he "obtained the Eucharist" [εὐχαριστίας ἐπιτυγχάνειν], which is to hear Mass.

units.la: VI.
units.tr: VI.

units.la: Post tempora Ambrosii adeò increbuit hujus vocis usus, ut viri docti, studio habentes loqui cum hominibus sui seculi, vocabula Græca ἐκκλησιάζειν, συναγειν, συναξις, λειτουργεῖν, λειτουργία, & apud Ignatium, δοχὴν ἐπιτελεῖν, per Missa, & Missas tenere exprimere non dubitârint, iis prædicationem verbi & administrationem sacramentorum significantes. Vulgo etiam Missa usurpata fuit pro solenni aliqua festivitate, sive die festo: ut quum in Capitulari Caroli M. legitur Missa Sancti Martini, pro die consecrato in honorem Martini, &c. Sant Martins/Sant Michels Mess/&c.
units.tr: After Ambrose's time the use of this word became so common that learned men, wishing to speak the language of their own age, did not hesitate to render the Greek words ἐκκλησιάζειν, συναγειν, συναξις, λειτουργεῖν, λειτουργία, and in Ignatius δοχὴν ἐπιτελεῖν, by "Missa" and "Missas tenere", meaning by them the preaching of the Word and the administration of the sacraments. Commonly too Missa was used for some solemn feast or festival day, as when in the Capitulary of Charlemagne we read "Missa Sancti Martini", meaning the day consecrated in honour of Martin, etc. Sant Martins/Sant Michels Mess/&c.

units.la: VII.
units.tr: VII.

units.la: Tandem Missa sumi cœpit ingenti degeneratione pro sacrificio externo proprie dicto, non modò μνημονευτικῷ, commemorativo vel repræsentativo sacrificii Christi in cruce peracti, nec modò εὐχαριστικῷ vel λατρευτικῷ, sed etiam verè ἱλαστικῷ: quo sacerdos filium Dei, sub speciebus panis & vini, Patri offerens, eum iratum propitiet, mereatur remissionem omnium peccatorum, & impetret bona cùm corporalia, tum spiritualia, pro vivis & defunctis: pro quibus fit Missa, vel quibus Missa applicatur.
units.tr: At last Missa began, through a huge degeneration, to be taken for an external sacrifice properly so called: not only the commemorative or representative sacrifice of Christ's sacrifice accomplished on the cross, nor only the eucharistic or latreutic sacrifice, but truly the propitiatory sacrifice, by which the priest, offering the Son of God under the species of bread and wine to the Father, appeases him when angry, earns the remission of all sins, and obtains good things, both bodily and spiritual, for the living and the dead, for whom the Mass is said or to whom the Mass is applied.

units.la: VIII.
units.tr: VIII.

units.la: Quo posteriore sensu Missæ nomen & rem; quæ hac innuitur, in Ecclesia Christiana, ferendam non esse, in præsenti συζητήσει, qua par est diligentia, comprobare libet: & duo quidè ejus descriptionis πρῶτα φύλλα, nempe Missam esse sacrificium externum proprie dictum, & Missam esse sacrificium ἱλαστικὸν sive propitiatorium, σπω Θεῷ, sumam refellenda. Omnia enim & singula membra, quæ in Missæ sacrificio justam reprehensionem merentur, excutere, præsentis institu- ti mei non est.
units.tr: In the present discussion I am pleased to show, with due care, that the Mass name and thing in this latter sense, which is implied here, is not to be tolerated in the Christian Church. I also wish to refute the two principal points of this description, namely that the Mass is an external sacrifice properly so called, and that the Mass is a propitiatory sacrifice offered to God. It is not part of my present purpose to examine all and each of the features of the Mass sacrifice that deserve just reproof.

units.la: PRIMO igitur pugnare cum veritate, Missam esse sacrificium externum proprie dictum, his potissimùm rationibus evincitur:
units.tr: PRIMO: first, that the Mass is an external sacrifice properly so called, which is contrary to the truth, is proved chiefly by these reasons:

units.la: 1. Si Christus in sacra Cœna non seipsum sacrificavit, aut se sacrificari mandavit Apostolis, sed sacramentum instituit corporis & sanguinis sui, hocq; præcepit in sui memoriam rite dispensari: tum sequitur, Missam; in quam illi sacram Cœnam transformant, sacrificium externum proprie dictum non esse: quandoquidem nullum opus proprie & per se potest esse sacramentum simul, & sacrificium.
units.tr: 1. If Christ in the holy Supper did not sacrifice himself, nor command the apostles to sacrifice him, but instituted a sacrament of his body and blood, and commanded that it be rightly dispensed in his memory, then it follows that the Mass, into which they transform that holy Supper, is not an external sacrifice properly so called, since no work can properly and of itself be a sacrament and a sacrifice at the same time.

units.la: Prius est verum, ex ipsa sacræ Cœnæ institutione.
units.tr: The first is true, from the very institution of the holy Supper.

units.la: Ergo verum est & posterius.
units.tr: Therefore the second is true too.

units.la: 2. Si in sacra Cœna neutrum symbolorum ita dispensatur, ut plane destruatur: tum sequitur, neq; sacrificium externum proprie dictum, quale volunt esse sacrificium Missæ, in ea peragi: quandoquidem, ipso Bellarmino teste, verum & reale sacrificium veram & realem mortem aut destructionem rei immolatæ desiderat.
units.tr: 2. If in the holy Supper neither of the symbols is dispensed so as to be utterly destroyed, then it follows that no external sacrifice properly so called, such as they want the Mass sacrifice to be, is performed in it, since, by Bellarmine's own testimony, a true and real sacrifice requires a true and real death or destruction of the thing offered.

units.la: Prius est verum. Ergo verum est & posterius.
units.tr: The first is true. Therefore the second is true too.

units.la: 3. Si Paulus in epistola ad Hebr. omnia sacrificiorum genera exponens, meminit duntaxat trium, nempe oblationum Testamentiveteris, oblationis Christi in cruce, & oblationem spiritualium novi: Missæ verò sacrificium prorsus tacet: tum sequitur, Missam nec proprium & externum, nec improprium & spirituale sacrificium esse.
units.tr: 3. If Paul in the epistle to the Hebrews, setting out all kinds of sacrifices, mentions only three, namely the offerings of the Old Testament, the offering of Christ on the cross, and the spiritual offerings of the New, but says nothing at all of a sacrifice of the Mass, then it follows that the Mass is neither a proper and external nor an improper and spiritual sacrifice.

units.la: Prius est verum. Ergo verum est & posterius.
units.tr: The first is true. Therefore the second is true too.

units.la: X. SECUNDO, pugnare cum veritate, Missam esse sacrificium propitiatorium, istis præcipuis rationibus comprobatur:
units.tr: X. SECONDLY, that the Mass is a propitiatory sacrifice, which is contrary to the truth, is proved by these chief reasons:

units.la: 1. Si Missa ne quidem est sacrificium: tum multò minùs erit sacrificium propitiatorium Testamenti novi.
units.tr: 1. If the Mass is not even a sacrifice, then much less will it be a propitiatory sacrifice of the New Testament.

units.la: Prius est verum: ut liquet ex rationibus commemoratis.
units.tr: The first is true, as is clear from the reasons already given.

units.la: Ergo verum est & posterius.
units.tr: Therefore the second is true too.

units.la: 2. Si sacrificium propitiatorium novi Testamenti est unicum & singulare, Christi videlicet oblatio semel facta in cruce; qua fideles in perpetuum expiati sunt a peccatis omnibus: Missa verò unica & singulris non est, sed varia & multiplex, & iterabilis in infinitum: tum sequitur, tur, hanc sacrificium propitiatorium novi Testamenti esse non posse: quandoquidem inter se pugnant, semel tantum &, saepius offerri: item, unica oblatione fideles in perpetuum a peccatis expiari, &, eandem oblationem quotidie continuari. Pugnantia autem simul stare nequeunt.
units.tr: 2. If the propitiatory sacrifice of the New Testament is unique and singular, namely Christ's offering made once for all on the cross, by which the faithful are cleansed from all sins for ever, but the Mass is not unique and singular, but varied, manifold and repeatable without end, then it follows that this cannot be the propitiatory sacrifice of the New Testament, since these things contradict each other: to be offered once only and to be offered often; likewise that the faithful are cleansed from sins for ever by a single offering, and that the same offering is continued daily. But contradictory things cannot stand together.

units.la: Prius est verum, juxta haec dicta: Hebr.7,26. & 27. Talis enim nos decebat pontifex: cui non sit quotidie necesse, quemadmodum illis pontificibus, prius pro peccatis propriis victimas offerre: deinde pro peccato populi. Id enim fecit SEMEL, quum semetipsum obtulit, &c. Et cap.9;12. Christus pontifex bonorum futurorum per proprium sanguinem ingressus est SEMEL in sacrarium, &c. Et verf.25. & 26. Nec enim necesse est, ut saepe offerat semetipsum sicut pontifex ingreditur in sacrarium quotannis cum sanguine alieno (alioquin oportuisset eum saepe passum fuisse a condito Mundo:) sed nunc SEMEL in consummatione saeculorum ad abolendum peccatum, per immolationem suiipsius patefactus est. Et verf.28. Christus SEMEL oblatus, ut multorum peccata tolleret, altera vice absque peccato conspicietur iis: qui ipsum exspectant ad salutem, &c. Item cap.10, v.10.12. & 14. Sanctificati sumus per oblationem corporis Iesu Christi SEMEL factam, &c. Hic vero UNA propecatis oblata victima in perpetuum sedet ad dextram Dei, &c. UNICA enim oblatione consecravit in perpetuum eos: qui sanctificantur, &c. His Paulinis oraculis succinit Augustinus l. 4. De Trin. c. 13. Morte sua, quippe UNO verissimo sacrificio, pro nobis oblato, quicquid culparum erat, unde nos principatus & potestates ad luenda supplicia iure detinebant, purgavit, abolevit, extinxit.
units.tr: The first is true, according to these sayings: Heb. 7:26 and 27. "For such a high priest became us, who has no need daily, as those priests did, to offer sacrifices first for his own sins and then for the sins of the people. For this he did ONCE, when he offered himself, etc." Also ch. 9:12. "Christ, the high priest of the good things to come, entered ONCE into the sanctuary through his own blood, etc." Also vers. 25 and 26. "For it is not necessary that he should offer himself often, as the high priest enters the sanctuary every year with the blood of another (otherwise he would have had to suffer often since the foundation of the world), but now ONCE at the end of the ages he has been revealed to put away sin by the sacrifice of himself." Also vers. 28. "Christ, offered ONCE to bear the sins of many, will appear a second time without sin to those who wait for him for salvation, etc." Likewise ch. 10, vers. 10, 12 and 14. "We have been sanctified through the offering of the body of Jesus Christ made ONCE, etc. But he, having offered one sacrifice for sins, sits for ever at the right hand of God, etc. For by ONE offering he has perfected for ever those who are sanctified, etc." Augustine agrees with these Pauline oracles, De Trinitate 4.13. "By his death, namely by ONE most true sacrifice offered for us, he purged, abolished and extinguished whatever guilt there was, by which the principalities and powers rightly held us to pay the penalty."

units.la: Ergo verum est & posterius:
units.tr: Therefore the second is true:

units.la: 3. Si sacrificium propitiatorium novi Testamenti, nempe Christi oblatio, semel facta in cruce, est vigoris perpetui & aeterni, quia nimirum sacerdos ille in aeternum vivit, & in aeternum perfectus est, nec non mediante hoc sacrificio crucis semper apparet vultui Dei pro nobis, Psalm. 110. Heb.7.9. & 10.cap. Missa vero isto vigore caret: tum sequitur, Missam sacrificium novi Test. propitiatorium non esse.
units.tr: 3. If the propitiatory sacrifice of the New Testament, namely Christ's offering made once on the cross, has a perpetual and eternal force, because that priest lives for ever and is perfected for ever, and by means of this sacrifice of the cross always appears before the face of God for us (Psalm 110; Heb. 7:9 and 10 ch.), but the Mass lacks this force, then it follows that the Mass is not the propitiatory sacrifice of the New Testament.

units.la: Prius est verum, juxta ilta dicta: Hebr.5,9. Et consecratus, factus est auctor salutis AETERNAE omnibus: qui ipsi auscultant. Et cap.9,12. AETERNAM redemtionem nobis est nactus, Et cap.10,14. Vnicâ oblatione IN PERPETVVM consecravit eos: qui sanctificantur. Quæ verba Ambrosius similitudine medicamenti illustrat. Vt enim, inquit, medicamentum quando fuerit forte, & salutis efficax, & valens cunctam valetudinem repellere, semel impositum totum operatur; ac proinde repeti quotidie non solet, sed si semper apponitur, manifestum indicium est, minùs illud prævaluisse: sic in Christo semel oblata hostia potens est ad salutem sempiternam, Quod Athanasius confirmat orat.3. contr. Arium, quum inquit: Salvatoris hostia semel oblata absolvit omnia, fidaq́ in omne tempus durat. Et Chrysostomus in cap.1.Iohan. hom.17. Sacrificium unum quidē tulit, sed semper per illud nos purgat. Quòd si ad hunc vigorem exigas sacrificium Missæ, vel ipsi Adversarii fateri coguntur, hoc adeò efficax non esse, quin infinitè repeti debeat, ad saltem unam animam e flammis Purgatorii extrahendam. Et vel a Deo ipso mandata sacrificia hoc nomine inefficacia & imperfecta fuisse, quia multa erant & iterabantur, ad Hebr.9. & 10. Apostolus colligit non semel.
units.tr: The first is true, according to these sayings: Heb. 5:9. "And being made perfect, he became the author of ETERNAL salvation to all who obey him." Heb. 9:12. "He obtained ETERNAL redemption for us." Heb. 10:14. "By one offering he has perfected FOR EVER those who are sanctified." Ambrose illustrates these words by the likeness of a medicine: for, he says, when a medicine is strong and effective for health, and able to drive out every sickness, once applied it works wholly; and therefore it is not usually repeated each day. But if it is always applied, that is a clear sign that it has not been strong enough. So in Christ a sacrifice offered once is powerful for eternal salvation. Athanasius confirms this in the third Oration against the Arians, when he says: "The Saviour's sacrifice, once offered, absolves all things and endures for all time." And Chrysostom on 1 John, homily 17: "He bore one sacrifice, but through it he always cleanses us." But if you require the Mass sacrifice to have this power, even the Adversaries are forced to admit that it is not so effective that it must be repeated endlessly, merely to draw even one soul out of the flames of Purgatory. And the sacrifices commanded by God himself were called ineffective and imperfect on this very account, because there were many and they were repeated; the Apostle infers in Heb. 9 and 10 that they were not once for all.

units.la: Ergo verum est & posterius.
units.tr: Therefore the second is true.

units.la: 4. Si sacrificium propitiatorium novi Testamenti necessariò requirit τλῶ αἱματοχυσίαν, sanguinis effusionem: in Missæ verò sacrificio ejusmodi effusio non fit, sed sacrificium ibi fingitur ἀναίμακτον, incruentum, & sine sanguine: tum sequitur eam sacrificium propitiatorium non esse.
units.tr: 4. If the propitiatory sacrifice of the New Testament necessarily requires bloodshedding [αἱματοχυσία], that is, an effusion of blood, but in the sacrifice of the Mass no such effusion takes place, and the sacrifice there is feigned to be unbloody [ἀναίμακτον], without blood, then it follows that it is not a propitiatory sacrifice.

units.la: Prius est verum, juxta hoc dictum: Hebr.9,22. Et absque sanguinis effusione non fit remissio. Vbi notandum, quòd Apostolus, ut significet, se non tantùm loqui de sacrificiis Iudaicis, jam abolitis, sed etiam de præsenti tempore, loquitur in præsenti, NON FIT remissio, &c. Et sanè sacrificia Legis propitiatoria non erant, nisi quando erant cruenta: ut significaretur, sacrificium etiam Christi cruentum esse debere, & sacrificium incruentum non esse sacrificium Christi.
units.tr: The first premise is true, according to this saying: Heb. 9:22. "And without shedding of blood there is no remission." Here it should be noted that the Apostle, to show that he is speaking not only of the Jewish sacrifices, now abolished, but also of the present time, speaks in the present tense: there IS no remission, etc. Indeed the sacrifices of the Law were not propitiatory except when they were bloody, so that it might be signified that the sacrifice of Christ too must be bloody, and that an unbloody sacrifice is not the sacrifice of Christ.

units.la: Ergo verum est & posterius. ˣ Si ubicunque est remissio peccatorum, ibi non est jam reliqua hostia pro peccato: tum sequitur, quia remissio ejusmodi est in solo & unico sacrificio Christi in cruce peracto, non vero in Missa, eam sacrificium propiatorium non esse.
units.tr: So the second premise is also true. If wherever there is remission of sins, there is no longer any remaining sacrifice for sin, then it follows that, since such remission is found only in the one sacrifice of Christ accomplished on the cross, and not in the Mass, the Mass is not a propitiatory sacrifice.

units.la: Prius est verum, juxta dictum: Hebr. 10, 8. Porrò ubi est peccatorum remissio, non est amplius oblatio pro peccato: ex natoria videlicet, vera & realis, seu actualis. Addit Theodoretus: Est enim supervacanea datâ remissione, &c. Et Chrysostomus: Si igitur dimisit peccata per unam hostiam, jam non amplius opus est secundâ, &c.
units.tr: The first premise is true, according to the saying: Heb. 10:8. "Moreover, where there is remission of sins, there is no longer any offering for sin": that is, an offering that is expiatory, true and real, or actual. Theodoret adds: "For it is superfluous, once remission has been given, etc." And Chrysostom: "If then he has forgiven sins through one sacrifice, there is no longer any need for a second, etc."

units.la: Ergo verum est & posterius.
units.tr: So the second premise is also true.

units.la: XI.
units.tr: XI.

units.la: ALIA argumenta brevitatis caussâ, & quod extent passim apud orthodoxos doctores, praetermitto. Placet jam praecipua σοφὰ φάρμακα Bellarmini paucis examinare, adque Lydium lapidem exigere, ut ex infirmitate τῆς ἐπιεικείας ἀσφαλίας magis firma fiat ὀρθολοξία. Hic ille, si usquam alibi, strenuum athletam agit, & pro Missa sacrificio, tanquam pro summo Ecclesia Romana Palladio omnibus viribus decertat, argumentis perpluribus in medium allatis: quae ordinis caussâ in quatuor classes possunt distribui. In prima continentur figurae veteris Testamenti; in altera ejusdem vaticinia; in tertia testimonia quaedam Testamenti novi; in quarta Patrum nonnullorum dicta.
units.tr: I pass over other arguments, both for the sake of brevity and because they are found everywhere among the orthodox teachers. It now pleases me to examine briefly the chief "wise remedies" (σοφὰ φάρμακα) of Bellarmine and to put them to the touchstone, so that, by the weakness of his (lenient) [τῆς ἐπιεικείας] defence, our orthodoxy (ὀρθολοξία) may become more firmly secure. Here he plays the vigorous athlete, if anywhere else, and fights with all his might for the sacrifice of the Mass, as for the chief Palladium of the Roman Church, bringing forward very many arguments. For the sake of order these can be distributed into four classes. The first contains the figures of the Old Testament; the second, its prophecies; the third, certain testimonies of the New Testament; the fourth, some sayings of the Fathers.

units.la: XII.
units.tr: XII.

units.la: Ad FIGURAS referuntur Melchisedeck, Agnus paschalis, sanguis sederis, & sacrificia.
units.tr: To the FIGURES are referred Melchizedek, the paschal lamb, the blood of the covenant, and the sacrifices.

units.la: XIII.
units.tr: XIII.

units.la: Quoad MELCHISEDECKVM, sic argumentatur Bellarminus: Christus est sacerdos secundùm ordinem Melchisedecki. Ordo hic consistit non tam in persona, & personae qualitatibus, quàm in sacrificio panis & vini, quod Melchisedeck peregit Gen. 14, 18.
units.tr: As to MELCHIZEDEK, Bellarmine argues thus: Christ is a priest according to the order of Melchizedek. This order consists not so much in the person and the qualities of the person as in the sacrifice of bread and wine, which Melchizedek performed (Gen. 14:18).

units.la: Ergo, ut typus compleatur, fatendum est Christum, etiam in ultima Coena sub speciebus panis & vini seipsum Deo obtulisse, idemque facere alios jussisse.
units.tr: Therefore, in order that the type may be fulfilled, it must be admitted that Christ, even at the last Supper, under the appearances of bread and wine, offered himself to God and commanded others to do the same.

units.la: Respondetur: Sacerdotium Christi secundùm ordinem Melchise-decki consistit in hoc, ut sicut Melchisedeck fuit rex justitiæ & pacis, rex & sacerdos Altissimi plane singularis, videlicet ἀπάτωρ, ἀμήτωρ, ἀγενεαλόγητος, neque initium habens dierum, neque finem vitæ, talis sit etiam Christus, rex quidem & sacerdos vera justitiæ & pacis, futurus ac mansurus in æternum, non iteratione (hæc enim imperfectionis est nota, Hebr. 7, 27. sed vigore & efficacia perpetuâ, Hebr. 10, 14.) ἀπάτωρ juxta humanitatem, ἀμήτωρ juxta deitatem; juxta quam est & ἀγενεαλόγητος, sine principio & fine, hoc est, immortalis & æternus Deus ipse. Sic enim explicatur Heb. 7, 3. Vbi notetur, quòd in tam diligenti descriptione, quam adeò præcisè & membratim persequitur Apostolus, ne quidem verbo tangit sacrificium Melchisedecki, in quo debeat obtulisse panem & vinum Deo; qui tamen id minimè prætermittere debuit, siquidem in sacrificii similitudine fuit aliqua typi ratio. Tractat enim ibi collationem duorum sacerdotum, Melchisedecki & Christi, & quid in suo sacerdotio simile dissimile uterque habeat, particulatim docet.
units.tr: The answer is this: The priesthood of Christ according to the order of Melchizedek consists in this, that just as Melchizedek was king of righteousness and peace, king and priest of the Most High, quite singular, namely fatherless, motherless, without genealogy (ἀπάτωρ, ἀμήτωρ, ἀγενεαλόγητος), having neither beginning of days nor end of life, so Christ too is such: king indeed and priest of true righteousness and peace, to be and to remain for ever, not by repetition (for this is a mark of imperfection, Heb. 7:27), but by perpetual power and efficacy (Heb. 10:14). He is fatherless according to his humanity, motherless according to his deity; and according to that deity he is also without genealogy (ἀγενεαλόγητος), without beginning and end, that is, he is God himself, immortal and eternal. For thus Heb. 7:3 is explained. Here it should be noted that in so careful a description, which the Apostle follows so precisely and point by point, he does not so much as touch on any sacrifice of Melchizedek in which he is supposed to have offered bread and wine to God; yet he ought by no means to have passed this over, since if there was a sacrifice, there was some element of typology in the resemblance of sacrifice. For there he treats the comparison of the two priests, Melchizedek and Christ, and teaches point by point what each has in his priesthood that is like or unlike.

units.la: 1. Hîc plura excipit Iesuita: & primò ait, Haud pertinuisse collationem sacrificii Melchisedecki cum sacrificio Christi adinstitutum Apostoli; quia ille docere tantum modò voluerit, ordinem Melchisedecki, juxta quem Christus est sacerdos, præstantiorem esse ordine Levitico, &c. Imò maximè pertinuit; quia ille prius exponit ex historia Melchisedecki, quis & qualis sit iste ordo. Atqui huc cumprimis attinuit exponere sacrificium panis & vini, si quod fuisset: quia Christi oblationem ac sacerdotium prolixè describit & urget. At panis & vini, aut oblationis a Melchisedecko factæ mentionem facit prorsus nullam.
units.tr: 1. Here the Jesuit raises several objections, and first he says that the comparison of Melchizedek's sacrifice with the sacrifice of Christ had nothing to do with the Apostle's purpose, since he wished only to teach that the order of Melchizedek, according to which Christ is a priest, is more excellent than the Levitical order, etc. Indeed it had very much to do with it, since he first sets out from the history of Melchizedek what this order is and what it is like. Now it was especially relevant to set out a sacrifice of bread and wine, if there had been one, since he describes and presses the offering and priesthood of Christ at length. But he makes no mention at all of any bread and wine, or of any offering made by Melchizedek.

units.la: 2. Secundò, In historia expresse haberi, Melchisedeckum obtulisse panem & vinum, &c. Non verò illa obtulit, hoc est, sacrificavit; sed protulit, pro regià nimirû suâ liberalitate, & antiquâ consuetudine, ad alimoniam sive refectionem Abrahæ & exercitus ejus. Id enim rei gestæ peristasis docet: & verbum הוציא hôtzi, quo Moses utitur, non offerre, hoc est, sacrificare, sed efferre, sive proferre, & educere, sive producere significat: ut Exod. 12, 51. Eduxit Iehova filios Israëli e terra Aegypti. 2. Sam. 12, 30. Eduxit spolia multa civitatis; Ier. 51, 10. Protulit Iehova justitias nostras. Sic Num. 20, 8, Psal. 135, 7. & alibi. & alibi. Unde Chaldæus interpres vertit אפיק, quod Guido Fabricius in lexico suo Syro-Chaldaeo reddit educere vel producere, a נפק exire, egredi, prodire, idem ac יצא, a quo fit והוציא; et Gracus ἐξήνεγκε: et Latinus protulit; et Germanus in Bibliis anno 1457. Augustæ Vind. impressis, er Bracht herfür, &c. quo etiam sensu interpretantur Cyprianus ad Cæcil. ep. 68. & Chrysostomus in Genes. hom. 35. & Iosephus antiq. lib. 1. c. 11, scribens: Melchisedeckum excepisse exercitum Abrahæ hospitaliter, nihilque eis ad victum deesse passum esse: & Philo, Eum mactatis victimis splendidum epulum sociis omnibus dedisse gratulabundum: & Ambrosius in cap. 7. ad Heb. Non esse novum, si Melchisedeck victori Abraham obviam processerit, & in refectionem tam ipsius, quam pugnatorum ejus, panem vinumque protulerit: & Epiphanius, qui tribus locis vertit ἐξήνεγκε, ἐξέβαλε, &c.
units.tr: 2. Secondly, he says that the history expressly states that Melchizedek offered bread and wine, etc. But he did not offer them, that is, sacrifice them; he brought them forth (protulit), out of his royal liberality and ancient custom, for the nourishment or refreshment of Abraham and his army. For the circumstances of the event show this, and the word הוציא (hotzi), which Moses uses, means not "to offer," that is, to sacrifice, but "to bring out," or "to bring forth," and "to lead out" or "to produce," as in Exod. 12:51: "The LORD brought out the sons of Israel from the land of Egypt"; 2 Sam. 12:30: "He brought out the great spoil of the city"; Jer. 51:10: "The LORD has brought forth our righteousness"; so also Num. 20:8, Ps. 135:7, and elsewhere. Hence the Chaldee interpreter renders it by אפיק, which Guido Fabricius in his Syro-Chaldaic lexicon gives as "to lead out or produce," from נפק, "to go out, to go forth, to come forth," the same as יצא, from which comes והוציא; and the Greek has ἐξήνεγκε [he brought out]; and the Latin protulit; and the German in the Bible printed at Augsburg in 1457 has "er bracht herfür" etc. In this same sense Cyprian (ad Caecilium, ep. 68), Chrysostom (in Genesin, hom. 35), and Josephus (Antiquities, book 1, ch. 11) interpret it, writing that Melchizedek received Abraham's army hospitably and allowed them to lack nothing for food; and Philo, that he gave a splendid feast to all his companions, having slain victims, in rejoicing; and Ambrose on chapter 7 of Hebrews: that it is not strange if Melchizedek went out to meet the victorious Abraham and brought forth bread and wine for the refreshment both of himself and of his fighting men; and Epiphanius, who in three places renders it by ἐξήνεγκε and ἐξέβαλε, etc.

units.la: 3. Tertiò, Verbum הוציא esse verbum sacrificale, ut Iud. 6, 18 ita hoc loco, &c. Sed nec illo loco sacrificale est: quoniam מנחה, qui cum jungitur, non sacrificium ibi notat, aut oblationem, sicut putat ille: sed cibum vel edulium, ad prandium paratum; quo Angelum Iehovæ reficere Gedeon cupiebat, postea et per otium de signo edendo cum eo acturus. Et si con edamus sacrificale esse: num propterea sequetur tale esse in loco Genesis: quum infinitis locis alius non sit; in quis rebus quibus vis, quæ educuntur, vel exportantur accommodatur? Unde vel ipso hoc loco non absolute, sed conjunctim cum voce commemorata מנחה usurpatur.
units.tr: 3. Thirdly, he says that the verb הוציא is a sacrificial verb, as in Judg. 6:18, so also here, etc. But not even in that passage is it sacrificial, since the מנחה which is joined with it there does not mean a sacrifice or an offering, as he thinks, but food or a meal prepared for dinner, with which Gideon wished to refresh the Angel of the LORD, intending afterwards to speak with him at leisure about giving a sign. And even if we grant that it is sacrificial there, does it follow that it is so in the passage of Genesis, since in countless places it is not so, and it is applied to any things which are brought out or carried out? Hence even in this passage it is used not absolutely, but in conjunction with the word מנחה just mentioned.

units.la: 4. Quartò, Abrahamum & milites ejus cibariis abundasse: quare supervacaneum fuisse, Melchisedeckum illa proferre, &c. Hic certum est, etsi id sci visseт Melchisedeck, voluisse tamen eum istâ μεγαλοπρεπεία suam erga Abrahamum benevolentiam, & ex victoria lætitiam declarare.
units.tr: 4. Fourthly, he says that Abraham and his soldiers had plenty of provisions, so that it was superfluous for Melchizedek to bring them forth, etc. Here it is certain that, even if Melchizedek knew this, he nevertheless wished to declare his goodwill towards Abraham, and his joy at the victory, by this magnificence.

units.la: 5. Quintò, Vulgatum interpretem reddere verba sequentia, והוא כהן, Erat enim sacerdos: quasi ideò panem & vinum sacrificârit Melchisedeck, quia fuerit sacerdos. Sed notandum in textu Hebraeo habere והוא, Erat autem, vel, Et erat: non, ut reddit ille, Erat enim. Unde Græci verterunt, ἦν ὁ ἱερεὺς: & Epiphanius καὶ ἦν ἱερεὺς: & Chaldæus, והוא משמש vehú meschámmesch, Et ipse minister: & Hieronymus epist. 126. ad Evagr. Erat autem sacerdos, &c. Particula enim causalis ςδ, vel, enim a nemine hic retinetur, neque a Cajetano ipso, quum inquit: Quòd autem in vulgata editione subditur ut causa oblationis, Erat enim sacerdos, &c. in Hebræo non habetur ut causa, sed ut separata clausula. quod & Arias in versione interlineari observat, transferens, Et ipse sacerdos, &c. Alio quin non negatur, vau quandoque causale fieri, ut Gen. 20, 3. Psal. 60, 13. et alibi. Sed id fit antecedentium ratione. Hic vero cur pro causali ponendum, in antecedentibus ratio est nulla. Nam quia Chaldæi, Græci, Latini, & plerique Patrum veterum, & recentium doctorum locum istum sic reddiderunt, Melchisedeck protulit panem & vinum: &, quod magis est, protulisse volunt ad reficiendum Abrahamum & exercitum ejus, e bello reducem; ac proinde non obtulisse, vel protulisse Deo: idcirco ridiculum foret consequentia transferre, Erat enim, &c. siquidem ut munificentiam illam declararet Melchisedeck erga Abrahamum, non erat opus, sacerdotem eum esse: quandoquidem eam declaravit ut rex, qualis revera fuit. Sed additum hoc est, propter consequentem ejus loci actum; quo dicitur Melchisedeck Abrahamo benedixisse, quod sacerdotum fuit munus singulare: quin etiam propter decimas; quas illi Abraham persolvit de præda sua; quas constat olim ex præscripto Dei sacerdotibus solutas esse.
units.tr: Fifthly, the Vulgate translator renders the following words, והוא כהן, as "For he was a priest," as though Melchizedek offered bread and wine precisely because he was a priest. But it must be noted that the Hebrew has והוא, "and he was" or "and he was indeed," not "for he was" as the Vulgate has it. Hence the Greeks rendered it "he was the priest" [ἦν ὁ ἱερεύς], Epiphanius "and he was a priest" [καὶ ἦν ἱερεύς], and the Chaldee paraphrast "and he himself was minister" [והוא משמש vehu meshammesh]. Jerome too, in letter 126 to Evagrius, has "Now he was a priest," and so on. The causal particle "for" [γάρ], or "for," is retained here by no one, not even by Cajetan himself, when he says: That in the Vulgate edition there is added, as the cause of the offering, "For he was a priest," and so on, is not in the Hebrew as a cause but as a separate clause. Arias also notes this in his interlinear version, rendering "And he himself was a priest," and so on. Otherwise it is not denied that the vau sometimes becomes causal, as in Genesis 20:3, Psalm 60:13, and elsewhere. But this happens by reason of what precedes. Here, however, there is no reason in what precedes for taking it as causal. For although the Chaldeans, the Greeks, the Latins, and most of the ancient Fathers and recent learned writers have rendered the passage thus, "Melchizedek brought out bread and wine," and, what is more, want him to have brought it out to refresh Abraham and his army returning from battle, and therefore not to have offered it or brought it out to God, it would be absurd to draw the inference "For he was," and so on. For to display Melchizedek's generosity towards Abraham, there was no need for him to be a priest, since he displayed it as a king, which in truth he was. But this has been added on account of the action that follows in the passage, where it is said that Melchizedek blessed Abraham, which was a singular office of priests; and also on account of the tithes which Abraham paid him from his spoil, which it is established were once paid to priests by God's command.

units.la: 6. Sextò, Patres nonnullos locum hunc de sacrificio panis & vini intellexisse, &c. Esto, intellexerint, hoc pane & vino Melchisedekiano præfiguratum fuisse sacramentum Eucharistiæ, & sacrificium in cruce peractum; nondum tamen inde sequitur, illos Missæ sacrificium, ut nunc celebratur, intellexisse. Deinde plures alii Patres commemorari possint, qui non de tali sacrificio, verùm de commeatu, qui Hebraismo trito innuitur pane & vino, locum illum exposuerunt; quos non minus Spiritu sancto; quàm alios, præditos fuisse constat. Adde quòd Patres suis interpretationibus sine scripturæ testimoniis fidei dogmata extruere nequeunt. Hæc de Melchisedecko.
units.tr: 6. Sixth, the Fathers, some of them, understood this passage of the sacrifice of bread and wine, and so on. Grant that they did understand it: that the sacrament of the Eucharist and the sacrifice accomplished on the cross were foreshadowed by Melchizedek's bread and wine; it still does not follow from this that they understood the sacrifice of the Mass as it is now celebrated. Moreover, many other Fathers might be cited who explained that passage not of such a sacrifice but of the provisions, indicated by the familiar Hebraism, of bread and wine; and it is clear that they were endowed with the Holy Spirit no less than the others. Add that the Fathers cannot build articles of faith from their own interpretations without the testimonies of Scripture. So much concerning Melchizedek.

units.la: XIV.
units.tr: XIV.

units.la: Quoad AGNVM PASCHALEM, contendit Bellarminus eum fuisse figuram Christi, jam verò ut Agnus manducabatur simul & immolabatur, ita corpus & sanguinem Christi in Missa, hoc est, est, sacra Cœna, non tantùm manducandum & bibendum, sed etiam immolandum esse, ut sit sacrificium propitiatorium pro peccatis vivorum & mortuorum.
units.tr: As for the PASCHAL LAMB, Bellarmine contends that it was a figure of Christ; and since the Lamb was both eaten and sacrificed at the same time, so the body and blood of Christ in the Mass, that is, in the Holy Supper, must not only be eaten and drunk but also be sacrificed, so that it may be a propitiatory sacrifice for the sins of the living and the dead.

units.la: Respond. Fuit sanè Agnus paschalis Christi figura, sed Christi immolatii in ara crucis, hoc est, rei in sacra Cœna significatæ. Nam diserte Paulus inquit: Pascha nostrum pro nobis sacrificatum est, Christus. Et Ioannes, Domine mactatus es, & redemisti nos Deo per sanguinem tuum, &c. Ubi neuter dicit, deinceps & quotidie sacrificandum aut mactandum esse: sed contrarium potiùs suadet Paulus, quum inquit: Festum agitemus non fermento veteri, nec fermento malitiæ & nequitiæ, sed azymis sinceritatis & veritatis. Atq; ita hanc figuram interpretatur Iustinus Martyr in Tryphone, Agnus ille, de quo ut assus totus fieret, præceptum est, supplicii crucis quod subiturus erat Christus, symbolum ac nota fuit: & Irenæus, lib. 4. cap. 23. Passus est Dominus, adimplens pascha: et Epiphanius hæres. 8. Erat illic Agnus irrationalis, qui sacrificabatur, deducens nos ad magnum Agnum & cœlestem, pro nob. & toto Mundo mactatum, &c.
units.tr: Reply. The paschal lamb was indeed a figure of Christ, but of Christ sacrificed on the altar of the cross, that is, of the thing signified in the Holy Supper. For Paul says plainly: "Christ our Passover has been sacrificed for us." And John: "Lord, you were slain and have redeemed us to God by your blood," and so on. Neither says that he is to be sacrificed or slain from then on and every day; Paul rather suggests the contrary when he says: "Let us keep the feast not with old leaven, nor with the leaven of malice and wickedness, but with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth." So Justin Martyr also interprets this figure in his Dialogue with Trypho: the lamb, whose whole roasting was commanded, was a symbol and sign of the death on the cross that Christ was to undergo. Irenaeus, book 4, chapter 23: "The Lord suffered, fulfilling the Passover." And Epiphanius, heresy 8: "There was there an irrational lamb which was sacrificed, leading us to the great and heavenly Lamb, slain for us and for the whole world," and so on. Anselm too, on 1 Corinthians 5: "The Passover of the Jews was the lamb immolated; our Passover is Christ immolated. For just as the Jews through the immolation of the lamb were freed from the power of Pharaoh and his soldiers, and so on, so we through the immolation of Christ have been freed from the power of the devil and his evil spirits." Thus concerning the paschal lamb.

units.la: 2. Quòd verò Patres nonnulli hunc Agnũ volunt etiam sacræ Cœnæ figurã fuisse: eo considerant celebrationẽ ejus ut actionẽ gratiarũ pro salute corporali Iudæorum ex Ægypto: non verò, quòd, ut Agnus fuit sacrificatus in mensa, ita Christus jam sacrificetur in ara. Nam, si proprie loquimur, Agnus ille non fuit sacrificium: quoniam nec per sacerdotes jugulabatur, nec in altari. Atqui id demum est sacrificium, inquit Bellarminus, quod proprie & per se pertinet ad actionem sacerdotis. Et nemo nescit Iudæos, etiam post abolita sacrificia, Agni celebrationem frequentâsse, et hodieq. frequentare. Sed esto, sacrificiũ fuerit, quid sequitur aliud, quàm Christũ de novo esse sacrificandũ, ut impleatur figura? Atqui is sacrificatus jam est, inquit Paulus. Et oportet sanguis ejus effundatur iterum, siquidem debet sacrificari: aliter sacrificium cruentum figura sacrificii incruenti esse nequeat. Faciunt huc Anshelmi verba: in 1. ad Cor. 5. Pascha Iudæorum immolatus est Agnus: pascha nostrum immolatus est Christus. Nam sicut Iudæi per immolationem Agni liberati sunt a potestate Pharaonis et satellitum ejus, &c. sic nos per immolationem Christi liberati sumus a potestate Diaboli, & spirituum malignorum ejus. Hac de Agno paschali.
units.tr: 2. But that some Fathers want this lamb also to have been a figure of the Holy Supper, they consider its celebration as a thanksgiving for the bodily salvation of the Jews from Egypt, not because, as the lamb was sacrificed at the table, so Christ is now sacrificed at the altar. For, speaking properly, that lamb was not a sacrifice, since it was neither slaughtered by priests nor at an altar. Yet, says Bellarmine, that alone is a sacrifice which properly and in itself belongs to the priest's action. And no one is unaware that the Jews, even after the sacrifices were abolished, have kept, and still keep, the celebration of the lamb. But grant that it was a sacrifice: what follows, other than that Christ must be sacrificed anew so that the figure may be fulfilled? Yet he has already been sacrificed, says Paul. And his blood would have to be poured out again, if he is to be sacrificed; otherwise a bloody sacrifice cannot be a figure of an unbloody sacrifice. The words of Anselm support this: on 1 Corinthians 5: "The Passover of the Jews was the lamb immolated; our Passover is Christ immolated. For just as the Jews through the immolation of the lamb were freed from the power of Pharaoh and his soldiers, and so on, so we through the immolation of Christ have been freed from the power of the devil and his evil spirits." Thus concerning the paschal lamb.

units.la: XV.
units.tr: XV.

units.la: Quoad SANGVINEM veteris foederis, Bellarminus ita argumentatur: Sanguis veteris foederis erat sanguis victimæ jam immolatæ. Ergo sanguis etiam novi foederis sanguis est victimæ immolatæ. Is autem sanguis est Christi, sicut ipsemet testatur. Ergo ipse fuit victima in Cœna immolata.
units.tr: As for the BLOOD of the old covenant, Bellarmine argues thus: the blood of the old covenant was the blood of a victim already sacrificed. Therefore the blood of the new covenant is also the blood of a sacrificed victim. But that blood is the blood of Christ, as he himself testifies. Therefore he himself was the victim sacrificed at the Supper.

units.la: Respond. Consequentia negatur. Nam sermo Christi de sanguine plane diversus est a sermone Moysis. Hic enim proprie loquitur; quia agit de vero sanguine pecudino, quo tunc vetus fœdus in præsenti actu sanciebatur: ille vero loquitur metonymicè, non quidem de sanguine suo, sed de symbolo duntaxat sanguinis sui, quo (videlicet, non jam symbolo, sed sanguine) novum fœdus paulò post sanciendum erat: sicut ex locorum collatione apparet. Hinc Paulus Heb.9. verba illa fœderis cum sacrificio crucis, ceu typum cum re significata, comparat manifestè: quicquid tandem Jesuita suis sex vel septem conditionibus, quas non in crucem, sed in Cœnam quadrare dicit, χειρὶ καὶ ποσὶ contranitatur.
units.tr: Reply. The inference is denied. For Christ's words about the blood are quite different from Moses' words. Moses speaks properly, because he deals with the true blood of a sheep or goat, by which the old covenant was then ratified in the present act; but Christ speaks metonymically, not indeed of his own blood, but only of the symbol of his blood, by which (namely, not now by symbol but by blood) the new covenant was to be ratified shortly afterwards, as appears from comparing the passages. Hence Paul in Hebrews 9 plainly compares those words of the covenant with the sacrifice of the cross, as a type with the thing signified. Whatever the Jesuit may contend with his six or seven conditions, which he says fit the Supper and not the cross, with hand and foot [χειρὶ καὶ ποσὶ].

units.la: XVI.
units.tr: XVI.

units.la: Quoad SACRIFICIA veteris Testamenti, sacrificium Christi variè præfigurantia, necnon utriusq; Testamenti proportiones, & cibi victimalis ac comestionis ipsius explicationes, quæ Jesuita affert, quia partim falsa, partim inepta sunt, ut ex locis ab eo citatis apparet, si modò singula seorsim diligenter inspiciantur: idcirco ea prætermitto, & ad alteram argumentorum classem; in qua vaticinia contineri dixi, progredior.
units.tr: As for the SACRIFICES of the Old Testament, which variously foreshadow the sacrifice of Christ, and likewise the correspondences of the two Testaments, and the explanations of the sacrificial food and of its eating, which the Jesuit brings forward: since they are partly false and partly absurd, as appears from the passages he cites, if each single point is examined carefully on its own, I therefore pass them over and proceed to the other class of arguments, in which I said the prophecies are contained.

units.la: XVII.
units.tr: XVII.

units.la: Ad VATICINIA referuntur.
units.tr: To PROPHECIES are referred.

units.la: Primò Locus 1.Sa.2.35. Et suscitabo mihi fidelē sacerdotē; qui indesinenter ambulet coram uncto meo, &c. Bellarminus hic intelligit Tzadokum & Christum, ab eo præfiguratū, & sacerdotes Christianos; qui, ut vaticinium compleant, sacrificium Missæ sint peracturi, &c.
units.tr: First, the passage 1 Sam. 2:35: "And I will raise up for myself a faithful priest, who shall walk before my anointed continually," etc. Bellarmine here understands Zadok, and Christ prefigured by him, and the Christian priests, who are to offer the sacrifice of the Mass, etc., in order to fulfil the prophecy.

units.la: Respond. Omnes illi sacerdotes rectè intelliguntur. Nam omnes fidele Deo sacerdotium peregerunt, hodieq; peragunt: Tzadok quidem, & posteri ejus, sacerdotium Aharonicum; Christus verò sacerdotium in cruce, adque se, adque dextram Patris: & Christiani sacerdotium spirituale; quod sanctimoniæ sacerdotium appellat Cyprianus: quo de sacerdotio & sacrificio Augustinus, & alii, hunc locum disertè exponunt. At sacrifi-cii Missæ quum hîc nec typus ullus exstet, nec vestigium aliquod impri-matur: ingens ἀσυλλογισία est, eam illis attribuere.
units.tr: Reply. All those priests are rightly understood. For all of them have performed the priesthood faithfully to God, and still do: Zadok and his descendants indeed the Aaronic priesthood; Christ the priesthood on the cross, and at the right hand of the Father; and Christians the spiritual priesthood, which Cyprian calls the priesthood of holiness. Augustine and others expound this passage clearly on this priesthood and sacrifice. But since no type of the sacrifice of the Mass is present here, nor any trace of it is stamped on the text, it is an enormous non sequitur [ἀσυλλογισία] to attribute it to them.

units.la: XVIII.
units.tr: XVIII.

units.la: Secundò Locus Prov.9,2. Sapientia, id est, Christus miscuit vi num suum, &c. Hinc dicit Bellarminus, quum ejusmodi mistio fiat in sacrificio Missæ, eam satis palàm inde confirmari.
units.tr: Second, the passage Prov. 9:2: "Wisdom, that is, Christ, has mixed her wine," etc. From this Bellarmine says that, since such a mixing is done in the sacrifice of the Mass, this is plainly confirmed from it.

units.la: Respond. Verbum מסך, quo Salomon utitur, declarat tam in-fundere, quàm miscere: prout Orientales, qui vina habebant admo-dum generosa, ea non nisi aquâ dilutâ infundebant. Iam verò infunde-re vinum, est largiri præstantia bona, Psal.23,5. Hæc bona Sapientiam, Christum ius dare docet Sapiens; qui ejus cognitionem hauriunt. Firmat hunc sensum animalium mactatio, & mensæ instructio; quorum itidem ibi fit mentio: quibus pariter bona ista innui, eodem ex Psalmo li-quet, ut & ex parabola Matt.22.&c. Hoc verò cum ἀνθρωπο παραβολῶ mistione in Missa fieri solita quid commune habet? Sed posito atq; con-cesso, de sacrificatione Christi ibilagi: quid aliud sequetur, quàm Sapienti-am, hoc est, Christum, sanguinem suum, cujus vinum in Eucharistia est sacramentum, fudisse in cruce, & corpus suum ibi mastâsse, indeq; bona omnis generis, quæ per mensam intelliguntur, ad nos redundare; ut quì-dem, Ioh.6,51,55. Hebr.13,10. & alibi, disertè explicatur?
units.tr: Reply. The word מסך [masak], which Solomon uses, means both to pour out and to mix, as the Orientals did, who, having very strong wines, poured them out only when diluted with water. Now to pour out wine is to bestow excellent blessings (Ps. 23:5). The wise man teaches that these blessings, Christ, are given to those who drink in the knowledge of him. The slaughter of the animals and the preparation of the table, which are likewise mentioned there, confirm this sense; and that these blessings are likewise meant there is clear from the same Psalm, and also from the parable in Matt. 22, etc. But what does this have in common with the mixing customarily done in the Mass? But even granting and conceding that the sacrifice of Christ is in view, what else would follow than that Wisdom, that is, Christ, poured out his blood on the cross (of which the wine in the Eucharist is the sacrament) and there consumed his body, and that from this all blessings of every kind, which are understood by the table, overflow to us? This is plainly explained in John 6:51, 55; Heb. 13:10, and elsewhere.

units.la: XIX.
units.tr: XIX.

units.la: Tertiò, Locus Esa.19,21. Aegyptii tempore illo Iehovam co-lent sacrificio, &c. Bellarminus hîc itidem Missæ sacrificium intelligit.
units.tr: Third, the passage Isa. 19:21: "The Egyptians in that time shall worship Jehovah with sacrifice," etc. Bellarmine here likewise understands the sacrifice of the Mass.

units.la: Respond. At Propheta intelligit sacrificia spiritualia, more inter Prophetas usitato; qui novi Testamenti cultum spiritualem designant externo culru veteris, et inprimis sacrificiis. Illa porrò sacrificia spiri-tualia sunt varia et multa, quando nimirũ homines fideles offerunt primò seipsos hostias vivas et rationales; de quib. Paulus, Sistite corpora ve-stra hostiâ vivam, sanctam, acceptâ Deo, rationalem illum cul-tum vestrum, &c. Et Petrus, Ipsi quoq; veluti vivi lapides ædifi-cati fiatis domus spiritualis, sacerdotium sanctum, ad offeren-dum spiritualia sacrificia, accepta Deo per IESVM Christum. Secundò ; quando offerunt ex Dei mandato quicquid boni acceperunt. Quo pertinent, 1. Sacrificium μνημονευτικὸν, sive ἀνάμνησις τῆς θυσίας, hoc est, interprete Augustino, memoria dominicæ passionis in Ecclesia celebrata; de qua 1. Cor. 11,24. Hoc facite ad mei recordationem. Quotiescunque enim ederitis panem hunc, & poculum hoc biberitis, mortem Domini annunciate usquequo venerit. 2. Sacrificium laudis, θυσίαι τῆς αἰνέσεως, ἀναίμοι καὶ ἀναίμακτοι, hoc est, incruentæ hostiæ dictæ Eusebio, Oecumenio, & aliis; quibus non tam de commemorato sacrificio Christi in cruce peracto, quàm de aliis beneficiis Deum celebramus, eiq; gratias agimus: quo de genere loquitur David, Immola Deo sacrificium laudis, &c. item, Et Magnificabo Deum, placebitq; ei super sacrificium vituli novelli, &c. item, Et sacrificabunt sacrificia laudis, &c. item, Voluntaria sacrificia oris mei accepta quæso Iehova, &c. Et Paulus, Per ipsum ergo offeramus sacrificium laudis, id est, fructum labiorum, &c. 3. Officia charitatis, θυσίαι τῆς εὐποιίας, erga pios, maximè erga verbi ministros & egenos: de quibus Paulus itidem, Expletus sum acceptis ab Epaphrodita, quæ a vobis allata sunt, in odorem bonæ fragrantiæ sacrificium acceptum, &c. item, Nam subministratio oblationis istius exundat per multas gratiarum actiones Deo, &c. item, Beneficentiæ autem & communionis nolite oblivisci: talibus enim sacrificiis delectatur Deus, &c. 4. Preces: de quibus iterum David, Dirigatur oratio mea sicut incensum in conspectu tuo: elatio manuum mearum sacrificium vespertinum. Et Iohannes, Data sunt ei suffimenta multa, ut ponerent ea cum precibus sanctorum omnium, &c. 5. Pœnitentia cum dolore, ex offenso Deo, violatâ lege, & peccati fœditate concepto; de quo David: Sacrificia Dei sunt spiritus fractus: animum fractum & contritum, o Deus, non spernis, &c. His omnibus accensetur prædicatio Evangelii; quam ejus ministri ipsi Deo offerunt: de qua Paulus, Ad hoc, ut sim minister Christi apud gentes, sacrificium offerens Evangelium Dei, &c. item, Si pro lamento offerar super hostia, sacrificio fidei vestræ gaudeo, &c. Vult dicere super prædicatione mea, qua vos in fidei obedientiam perduxi, adeóq. obtuli & sacrificavi, &c. In quæ verba Chrysostomus, Meum est, inquit, prędicare & evangelizare: machæra siquidem mea est Evangeliū, prædicationis videlicet sermo, &c. Nec obstat, quod regerit Adversarius, Hoc modo discrimen nullum fore inter ministros verbi, & reliquos fideles, &c. Imò discrimen est ingens ratione ministerii; cujus multæ sunt partes, quæ reliquos fideles non tangunt, licet discrimen non sit ratione sacerdotii, quod omnium fidelium in novo Testamento est commune.
units.tr: Reply. But the prophet means spiritual sacrifices, in the manner usual among the prophets, who designate the spiritual worship of the New Testament by the outward ceremony of the Old, and especially by sacrifices. Those spiritual sacrifices are various and many: first, when faithful men offer themselves as living and rational victims; of which Paul says, "Present your bodies a living sacrifice, holy, acceptable to God, which is your rational worship," etc. And Peter: "You also, like living stones, are built up into a spiritual house, a holy priesthood, to offer spiritual sacrifices acceptable to God through Jesus Christ." Second, when by God's command they offer whatever good they have received. To this belong: (1) the memorial sacrifice [μνημονευτικὸν], or remembrance of the sacrifice [ἀνάμνησις τῆς θυσίας], that is, in Augustine's words, the memory of the Lord's passion celebrated in the Church; of which 1 Cor. 11:24: "Do this in remembrance of me. For as often as you eat this bread and drink this cup, you proclaim the Lord's death until he comes." (2) The sacrifice of praise [θυσίαι τῆς αἰνέσεως], bloodless and unbloody [ἀναίμοι καὶ ἀναίμακτοι], that is, the unbloody victims called so by Eusebius, Oecumenius and others, by which we celebrate God and give him thanks not so much for the commemorated sacrifice of Christ accomplished on the cross as for other benefits. David speaks of this kind: "Offer to God the sacrifice of praise," etc.; likewise, "And I will magnify God, and it will please him more than the sacrifice of a young bullock," etc.; likewise, "And they shall offer sacrifices of praise," etc.; likewise, "Accept, I pray, O Jehovah, the freewill sacrifices of my mouth," etc. And Paul: "Through him then let us offer the sacrifice of praise, that is, the fruit of lips," etc. (3) Works of charity [θυσίαι τῆς εὐποιίας], toward the godly, and especially toward ministers of the Word and the needy; of which Paul likewise: "I am full, having received from Epaphroditus what was sent by you, a sacrifice acceptable and well pleasing to God," etc.; likewise, "For the ministering of this offering not only supplies the needs of the saints but also overflows through many thanksgivings to God," etc.; likewise, "But do not forget to do good and to share, for with such sacrifices God is pleased," etc. (4) Prayers: of which David again: "Let my prayer be set before you as incense, the lifting up of my hands as the evening sacrifice." And John: "Much incense was given to him, that he might offer it with the prayers of all the saints," etc. (5) Repentance with sorrow, conceived from having offended God, violated the law, and the foulness of sin; of which David: "The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit; a broken and contrite heart, O God, you will not despise," etc. To all these is added the preaching of the Gospel, which its ministers offer to God himself; of which Paul: "That I might be a minister of Christ to the Gentiles, offering the Gospel of God as a sacrifice," etc.; likewise, "But even if I am poured out as a drink offering upon the sacrifice of your faith, I rejoice," etc. He means: upon my preaching, by which I led you to obedience of faith, and so offered and sacrificed you, etc. On these words Chrysostom says, "It is mine," he says, "to preach and to evangelize: for the sword of the Gospel is mine, that is, the word of preaching," etc. Nor does it stand in the way that the adversary objects, that in this way there would be no distinction between ministers of the Word and the other faithful, etc. Indeed there is a great distinction by reason of the ministry, which has many parts that do not touch the other faithful, although there is no distinction by reason of the priesthood, which is common to all the faithful in the New Testament.

units.la: XX.
units.tr: XX.

units.la: Atq; his sacrificiis spiritualibus cùm Aegyptios, tum alias gentes, ad Christum convertendas, Deum culturas esse Esaias & cap. 19. vaticinatur, & cap. 56, 7. & 61, 6. & 66, 2. &c. Hinc Cyprianus inquit, A Christo dicuntur Christiani, ut sint sui, Christo duce, rectores & duces, & offerant Deo sacrificium quotidianum, ordinati a Deo sanctimoniæ sacerdotes. Et Cyrillus, Oratio hæc, tanquam ab exemplo & typo legalis cultus sumta est. Nam olim arietes & hircos incendere, & sacrificia offerre soliti sunt Israëlitæ: sed quoniam umbra transiit, non per sanguines aditum sibi faciunt ex gentib. vocati, sed veluti seipsos Deo sacrificant, Mundo morientes, justitiæ viventes, &c. Quòd verò altaris & statuæ meminit Esaias: ibi per signum & monimentum religionis intelligit ipsum ejus cultum, exercitium atq; professionem.
units.tr: And that these spiritual sacrifices are the worship of God by which the Egyptians, and other nations too, are to be converted to Christ, Isaiah prophesies, and also in chapters 19, 56:7, 61:6 and 66:2, and so on. Hence Cyprian says: "They are called Christians from Christ, so that, with Christ as their leader, they may be his rulers and commanders, and offer to God a daily sacrifice, priests ordained by God for holiness." And Cyril: "This prayer is taken as from the pattern and type of the legal worship. For the Israelites were once accustomed to burn rams and goats and to offer sacrifices; but since the shadow has passed away, those called from the Gentiles do not make their way to God through blood, but offer themselves to God as a sacrifice, dying to the world, living to righteousness, and so on." As for Isaiah's mention of an altar and a pillar, he understands by this sign and monument of religion the worship itself, its practice and its profession.

units.la: XXI.
units.tr: XXI.

units.la: Quartò ad vaticinia refertur locus Dan. 12, 11. A tempore, quum ablatum fuerit juge sacrificium, & posita fuerit abominatio in desolationem dies mille ducenti nonaginta, &c. Hîc Bellarminus per juge sacrificium vult significari sacrificium quotidianũ Missæ.
units.tr: Fourthly, the passage Daniel 12:11 is brought forward as a prophecy. "From the time that the continual sacrifice is taken away, and the abomination is set up for desolation, there shall be a thousand two hundred and ninety days," and so on. Here Bellarmine wants the continual sacrifice to mean the daily sacrifice of the Mass.

units.la: Respond. Vox sacrificium in textu Hebræo non habetur, sed tantùm vox juge: unde tam per vocem cultus, quàm per sacrificium potest suppleri: ut certè Hieronymus cultum Dei interpretatur. Id verò satis arguit, debili admodum fundamento niti Missam verbo, quod per supplementum in textum irrepsit. Verumenimverò Danielem hîc loqui de abolitione jugis sacrificii veteris Iudaici, non novi, aut Missæ, apparet ex alio ejus loco; qui exstat cap. 11, 31. Et polluent sanctuarium fortitudinis, & auferent juge sacrificium, & dabunt abominationem in desolationem, &c. Hîc partim interruptionem jugis sacrificii in Ecclesia Iudaica per Antiochum factam, partim abolitionem ejus in excidio Hierosolymæ, indicari, Dominus ipse explicat Matt. 24, 15. & ejus expositionem merito sequuntur Origines, Chrysostomus, & his similes.
units.tr: Reply: The word "sacrifice" is not found in the Hebrew text, only the word "continual"; so the word "worship" or "sacrifice" may be supplied. Jerome indeed interprets it as the worship of God. But this sufficiently shows that the Mass rests on a very weak foundation, namely a word which has crept into the text by supplement. Indeed, that Daniel here speaks of the abolition of the continual sacrifice of the old Jewish covenant, and not of the new one or of the Mass, is clear from another passage of his, which stands in chapter 11:31: "And they shall pollute the sanctuary of strength, and take away the continual sacrifice, and they shall set up the abomination of desolation," and so on. Here the interruption of the continual sacrifice in the Jewish Church, brought about by Antiochus, is partly indicated, and partly its abolition at the destruction of Jerusalem; the Lord himself explains this in Matthew 24:15, and Origen, Chrysostom and those like them rightly follow his exposition.

units.la: XXII.
units.tr: XXII.

units.la: Quintò Locus Mal. 1, 11. In omni loco sacrificatur & offertur nomini meo oblatio munda, &c. Bellarminus Missæ sacrificium necessariò hîc intelligendum esse multis argumentis conatur probare.
units.tr: Fifthly, the passage Malachi 1:11: "In every place incense is offered to my name, a pure offering," and so on. Bellarmine tries to prove by many arguments that the sacrifice of the Mass must necessarily be understood here.

units.la: Respond. At nos dicimus cum orthodoxa Antiquitate sacrificium intelligi spirituale. Cujus generis sunt sacrificia τῆς εὐχαριστίας καὶ ἱλα-σμοῦ καὶ μεταδοσίας: quæ γνῶσια novi Testamenti sacrificia esse supra est declaratum, & hoc loco per מִקְטִיר incensum seu suffitum, & per מִנְחָה oblationem seu προσφορὰν manifestè notantur: per illud quidem preces, per hoc verò cætera sacrificia; quæ munda dicta, quia sunt in Christo per fidem mundata; ac proinde etiam Deo grata, sicut Hebr. 13. & alibi docetur. Sed præter activa ista, passivum etiam sacrificium potest intelligi; quo ipsæ gentes per prædicationem Evangelii Deo prædicuntur offerendæ, hoc est, adducendæ, convertendæ & sanctificandæ: ut quidem Paul. Rom. 15, 16. & Phil. 2, 17. hunc locum non obscurè interpretatur. Non igitur visibile et externum sacrificium intelligit Propheta, sed illud potius abrogandum esse prædicit.
units.tr: Reply: But we say, with orthodox antiquity, that a spiritual sacrifice is meant. Of this kind are the sacrifices of thanksgiving, of propitiation and of communication [τῆς εὐχαριστίας καὶ ἱλασμοῦ καὶ μεταδοσίας], which, as was declared above, are the sacrifices of the New Testament; and in this passage they are plainly indicated by the incense or fumigation [מִקְטִיר] and by the offering or oblation [מִנְחָה, προσφορά]: the former indeed means prayers, the latter the other sacrifices; these are called pure because in Christ they are cleansed through faith, and therefore are also acceptable to God, as Hebrews 13 and elsewhere teaches. But besides these active sacrifices, a passive sacrifice can also be understood, by which the Gentiles themselves are offered to God through the preaching of the Gospel, that is, are brought, converted and sanctified. Paul indeed, Romans 15:16 and Philippians 2:17, interprets this passage not obscurely. The Prophet therefore does not mean a visible and external sacrifice, but rather foretells that it is to be abrogated.

units.la: XXIII.
units.tr: XXIII.

units.la: Bellarminus perplura hic excipit, ut Missam a Malachia intelligi probet: Et primum quidem argumentum petit ex voce מנחה oblatio: alterum ex voce טהרה munda: & tertium ex consensu Patrum.
units.tr: Bellarmine here raises very many points, to prove that the Mass is meant by Malachi. And first he takes an argument from the word מנחה, "offering"; a second from the word טהרה, "pure"; and a third from the agreement of the Fathers.

units.la: 1. Quoad primum: dicit מנחה absolutè hîc poni: ac proinde sacrificium intelligi proprium: quum spiritualia significentur semper cum adjuncto aliquo nomine, ut sacrificium laudis, justitiæ, etc. Resp. Id verò falsum est, quūm מנחה positum sit cum adjuncto nomine טהרה munda. 2. מנחה proprie esse sacrificium externum, e similaque oleo, thure, proindeque non spirituale, &c. Resp. Sumitur vox illa aut propriè, aut tropicè: propriè sumi hîc nequit; quia Propheta vaticinatur de oblatione Test. novi: in hoc verò sacrificia legalia a Christo abolita sunt. Tropicè igitur sumenda pro cultu spirituali, more apud Prophetas trito: qui, ut antè monui, de gentium vocatione verba facientes, cultum spiritualem, ad quem illas hortantur, ritu legis externo desig-
units.tr: 1. As to the first: he says that מנחה is here used absolutely, and therefore a proper sacrifice is meant, since spiritual things are always signified with some added noun, such as a sacrifice of praise, of righteousness, and so on. Reply: This is false, since מנחה is here placed with the added word טהרה, "pure". 2. He says that מנחה properly means an external sacrifice, of fine flour, oil and incense, and therefore not spiritual, and so on. Reply: That word is taken either properly or figuratively. It cannot be taken properly here, because the Prophet is prophesying about the offering of the New Testament, and in this the legal sacrifices have been abolished by Christ. It must therefore be taken figuratively, for spiritual worship, after the common manner of the Prophets, who, as I said before, when speaking of the calling of the Gentiles, point by the external rite of the law to the spiritual worship to which they exhort them.

units.la: nane nant. 3. Res futuras ritib. legis tum demum innui, quando res, quę significantur, tunc, quum describuntur, non fuerint in usu. Iam verò spiritualia sacrificia, hymnos, preces & alia, ubiq; & semper in usu fuisse. Hæc igitur nō per מנחה significari, ac proinde novū & antea inusitatū sacrificiū intelligi, etc. Resp. Sacrificium spirituale, de quo loquitur Malachias, Veterib. novū & inusitatum fuit juxta circumstantias, quas ibi memorat: nempe quòd absq; ceremoniis externis Leviticis, quæ in novo Testamento nunc sublata sunt, celebrandum erat in spiritu & veritate: neque jam uno loco, & ab una gente, sed ubiq;, & ab omnibus; ad quos vox Evangelii in toto orbe esset ventura: ut vel textus ipse docet, quando gentium, ortus & occasus solis, & loci omnis fit mentio. Unde Irenæus, Oblationes hîc, oblationes illic: sacrificia in populo Israël, sacrificia in ecclesia: sed species tantùm immutata est, quippe quum jam non a servis, sed a liberis offerantur. Et Chrysostomus novum sacramentū vocat, quod a nova mente proficiscitur, nec igni & fumo, sed gratiâ & spiritu Dei offertur, &c.
units.tr: 3. He says that future things are signified by the rites of the law only when the things signified were not yet in use at the time they are described. But spiritual sacrifices, hymns, prayers and other things have always been in use everywhere. Therefore these are not signified by מנחה, and so a new sacrifice, previously unused, is meant, and so on. Reply: The spiritual sacrifice of which Malachi speaks was new and unusual for the men of old, according to the circumstances he there records: namely, that it was to be celebrated in spirit and in truth, without the external Levitical ceremonies, which are now removed in the New Testament; and not now in one place and among one nation, but everywhere and by all, to whom the voice of the Gospel was to come throughout the whole world; as the text itself teaches, when it mentions the rising and setting of the sun among the Gentiles, and every place. Hence Irenaeus: "Offerings here, offerings there; sacrifices among the people of Israel, sacrifices in the Church; but only the form is changed, since they are now offered not by slaves but by free men." And Chrysostom calls it a new sacrament, which proceeds from a new mind, and is offered not with fire and smoke but by the grace and Spirit of God, and so on.

units.la: 2. Quoad alterum argumentum: dicit, Spiritualia sacrificia, quæ sunt opera nostra, per oblationem mundam intelligi non posse, quum sint immunda, &c. Resp. Tametsi fidelium sacrificia seu opera sunt immunda, quia imperfecta: tamen quia Deo per Christum offeruntur, defectus eorum non imputatur, sed munda, Deoq; accepta habentur propter Christum. Unde David, Lavabis me: & ero nive candidior. Sic Eusebius preces nostras mundum sacrificium vocat: & Tertullianus ad Scapulam Sacrificamus, inquit, pro salute Imperatoris pură prece, &c. Replicat ille, reputandi aut imputandi verbū a Malachia non usurpari. Sed sciat Iesuita, eo nos uti cum eodem Irenæo, sic scribente, Ecclesiæ oblatio, quam Dominus docuit offerri in universo Mundo, purum sacrificium reputatum est apud Deum, & acceptū est ei: non quòd indigeat a nob. sacrificium: sed quoniam is, qui offert, glorificatur ipse in eo, quod offert, si acceptetur munus ejus, etc. Deinde non pugnant, Est munda oblatio: & Deus reputat mundam. Est enim is: cui a Deo per Christum imputatur munditia, reipsa mundus, non ὁμωνύμως, quo modo Apostoli mundi dicti: sanè non naturâ, sed imputatione propter fidem in Christum: ob quam revera ipsi & omnes fideles mundi dici possunt.
units.tr: 2. As to the second argument: he says that spiritual sacrifices, which are our works, cannot be understood as a pure offering, since they are impure, and so on. Reply: Although the sacrifices or works of the faithful are impure, because imperfect, yet because they are offered to God through Christ, their defects are not imputed, but they are held pure and acceptable to God on account of Christ. Hence David: "Thou shalt wash me, and I shall be whiter than snow." So Eusebius calls our prayers a pure sacrifice; and Tertullian, in his letter to Scapula: "We sacrifice," he says, "for the safety of the Emperor, with pure prayer," and so on. He replies that the words "reckon" or "impute" are not used by Malachi. But let the Jesuit know that we use it together with the same Irenaeus, who writes thus: "The offering of the Church, which the Lord taught to be offered throughout the whole world, has been reckoned a pure sacrifice before God, and is accepted by him; not because God needs a sacrifice from us, but because he who offers is himself glorified in what he offers, if his gift is accepted," and so on. Then, "It is a pure offering" and "God reckons it pure" do not conflict. For he is truly pure to whom purity is imputed by God through Christ, pure in fact, not homonymously, as the Apostles were called pure; certainly not by nature, but by imputation on account of faith in Christ; on account of which all the faithful can truly be called pure.

units.la: 3. Quoad tertium: dicit, Iustinum, Irenæum, Tertullianum, & alios locum Malachiæ de sacrificio Eucharistiæ intellexisse. Respond.
