Si Patrum istorum verba examinentur; constabit eos, quando de Eucharistia loquuti sunt, sacrificium intellexisse spirituale, quod Deo a fidelibus in memoriam & celebrationem sacrificii in cruce facti offertur. Et nominatim Hieronymus per oblationem intelligit victimas spirituales; & Tertullianus, gloriæ relationem, benedictionem, laudem & hymnos: & Clemens Romanus orationes seu preces; quomodo idem Tertullianus & Hieronymus interpretantur. Quibus accenseri debet Chaldæus, interpres optimi commatis: Ego recipiam preces vestras, & nomen meum magnum sanctificabitur, & oratio vestra erit sicut oblatio munda coram me, &c. Progrèdior ad tertiam classem; in qua testimonia quædam novi T. continentur.
units.tr: 3. As to the third: he says that Justin, Irenaeus, Tertullian and others understood the passage of Malachi to be about the sacrifice of the Eucharist. Reply: If the words of those Fathers are examined, it will be clear that when they spoke of the Eucharist they understood a spiritual sacrifice, which is offered to God by the faithful in memory and celebration of the sacrifice made on the cross. And Jerome by name understands the offering to be spiritual victims; Tertullian understands the giving of glory, blessing, praise and hymns; and Clement of Rome understands prayers or supplications; as Tertullian and Jerome themselves interpret. To these should be added the Chaldee paraphrast, an excellent interpreter of this verse: "I will accept your prayers, and my great name shall be sanctified, and your prayer shall be like a pure offering before me," and so on. I now proceed to the third class, in which certain testimonies of the New Testament are contained.

units.la: XXIV. Ad TESTIMONIA novi Testamenti referuntur.
units.tr: XXIV. The passages of the New Testament are referred to.

units.la: Primò ipsa sacræ Cœnæ verba, Hoc est corpus meum: quod pro vobis traditur vel frangitur: item, Hoc est sanguis meus, qui pro vobis effunditur, &c. Hinc infert Bellarminus: Ergo jam tum, quum Dominus mensæ assideret, ipse corpus suum obtulit, & sanguinem suum fudit, sub speciebus nimirum panis & vini; idq. fieri jussit ab Apostolis, & eorum successoribus.
units.tr: First, the very words of the holy Supper: "This is my body, which is given or broken for you," and likewise "This is my blood, which is poured out for you," etc. From these Bellarmine infers: "Therefore already then, while the Lord was sitting at table, he offered his body and poured out his blood, namely under the species of bread and wine; and he commanded the Apostles and their successors to do the same."

units.la: Respond. Panis dicitur corpus Domini, & Poculum sanguis Domini, ratione sacramentali; qua symbolum non mutatur in rem: sed res per symbolum repræsentatur, offertur, obsignatur, hoc est, significantibus, ut loquitur Cyprianus, tribuuntur nomina significatorum, per metonymiam signi & signati. Unde Theodoretus: Servator quidem certè nostrer nomina commutavit, & corpori quidem id, quod erat symboli ac signi, nomen imposuit: symbolo autem quod erat corporis. Ita quum se vitem nominavisset, sanguinem, id quod erat symbolum, appellavit, &c. Et paulò post: Is symbola & signa, quæ videntur, appellatione corporis & sanguinis honoravit, non naturam quidem mutans, sed naturæ gratiam adijciens. Astipulatur Augustinus: Solet res, quæ significat ejus rei nomine, quam significat, nuncupari, sicut scriptum est, septem spicæ septem anni sunt, &c. Et mox: Hinc est, quod dictum ctum est, Petra erat Christus, &c. Item alibi: Hæc enim sacra-menta sunt; in quibus non quid sint, sed quid ostendant semper attenditur: quoniã signa sunt rerum aliud exsistentia, & aliud significantia, &c. Ob hanc rationẽ idem Patres & alii panem Eucha-risticum dicunt esse sacramentum, mysterium, symbolum, typum, antity-pum, figuram, signum, imaginem, similitudinem, memoriam, recordatio-nem corporis Christi, seu, quod eodem redit, significare, designare, ostende-re, repræsentare corpus Christi: quo sensu vinum Eucharistiæ est Christi sanguis. Hinc etiam Circumcisio vocatur fœdus: agnus, transitus: arca, Dominus; terra Canaan, requies Domini; Christus, petra; Christi caro, manna, & id genus sexcenta. Nequaquam igitur reale, exter-num & proprië dictum sacrificium illis verbis instituitur, sed sacrificii in cruce peracti recordatio; quam non solus sacerdos, sed tota Ecclesia Deo offert, laudis videlicet sacrificium, & verè εὐχαριστικόν.
units.tr: Answer: Bread is called the body of the Lord, and the cup the blood of the Lord, by a sacramental reckoning, by which the sign is not changed into the thing. Rather, the thing is represented, offered and sealed through the sign. That is, the names of the things signified are given to the signs, as Cyprian says, by a metonymy of sign and thing signified. Hence Theodoret: "Our Saviour indeed changed the names: to the body he gave the name that belonged to the symbol and sign, and to the symbol the name that belonged to the body. So when he called himself a vine, he called the blood what was the symbol, etc." And a little later: "He honoured the symbols and signs, which are seen, with the title of body and blood, not changing their nature, but adding grace to nature." Augustine agrees: "The thing that signifies is usually named by the name of the thing it signifies, as it is written, the seven ears are seven years, etc." And soon after: "Hence it is said, The rock was Christ, etc." Likewise elsewhere: "For these are sacraments, in which one always attends not to what they are but to what they show; for they are signs, existing as one thing and signifying another, etc." For this reason the same Fathers and others call the Eucharistic bread a sacrament, mystery, symbol, type, antitype, figure, sign, image, likeness, memorial, remembrance of the body of Christ; or, which comes to the same thing, to signify, designate, show, or represent the body of Christ. In this sense the wine of the Eucharist is the blood of Christ. Hence also circumcision is called a covenant; the lamb, a passover; the ark, the Lord; the land of Canaan, the rest of the Lord; Christ, a rock; Christ's flesh, manna, and countless such things. By no means, therefore, is a real, external and properly so-called sacrifice instituted by those words, but a remembrance of the sacrifice accomplished on the cross. This is offered to God not by the priest alone but by the whole Church, namely the sacrifice of praise, and truly eucharistic [εὐχαριστικόν].

units.la: 2. His non obstat verborum, datur, frangitur, effunditur, præ-sens usurpatio. Est enim ibi enallage temporum, scripturæ usitata; quæ de futuro perinde, ac de præsenti, loquitur, ob majorem rei mox futuræ cer-titudinem & evidentiam, nec non ob spiritualem & efficacem veræ fidei naturam; quæ res certò futuras, non minus ac præteritas, efficaciter ap-prehendit. Hinc interpres Hebræus Evangelii Matthæi verba illa ex-pressè in futuro tempore usurpavit: & vulgatus Latinus reddidit apud Matth. & Lucam, effundetur; quod faciunt & Origenes, Chrysosto-mus & alii. Non obstat etiam frangendi verbum apud Paulum, quasi Christi oblatio in sacræ Cœnæ usu fuerit facta verè & realiter: maximè quum corpus Christi in cruce non fractum dicatur Iohan. 19. Nam fra-ctio in verbis sacræ Cœnæ metaphoricè est ipsa Christi crucifixio & mors; in qua verè corpus Christi laceratum, hoc est, clavis contusum & lanceâ perfossum, sicq. fractum perhibetur, Psal. 22. Esa. 53. &c. Agit verò Iohannes tantùm de fractione crurum sive comminutione ossium propriè dicta.
units.tr: 2. None of this is hindered by the use of the present tense in the words "is given," "is broken," "is poured out." For there is an enallage of tenses, customary in Scripture, which speaks of the future just as it does of the present, on account of the greater certainty and evidence of what is about to come, and also on account of the spiritual and effective nature of true faith, which grasps things certainly future no less effectively than things past. Hence the Hebrew translator of Matthew's Gospel expressly used the future tense in those words, and the Latin Vulgate rendered it "will be poured out" in Matthew and Luke. Origen, Chrysostom and others do the same. Nor is it hindered by the word "broken" in Paul, as if Christ's offering had been truly and really made in the use of the holy Supper, especially since Christ's body is said in John 19 not to have been broken on the cross. For breaking in the words of the holy Supper is, metaphorically, Christ's crucifixion and death itself, in which his body was truly torn, that is, bruised by nails and pierced by a lance, and so is said to be broken (Ps. 22; Isa. 53, etc.). John, however, speaks only of the breaking of the legs, or the crushing of bones, in the proper sense.

units.la: XXV.
units.tr: XXV.

units.la: Secundò, Locus Act. 13,2. ubi Apostoli dicûtur λειτουργοῦντες. Hic Bellar. asserit, λειτουργίαν sacrificium significare & hodie̦ Græcis esse idem, quod Latinis est sacrificium Missæ, & Syris מתחבשפנרתא methcaschphanuta. Unde colligit, etiam Apostolos olim sacrificâsse, hoc est, Christum in S. Cœna obsculisse: quum nullum aliud genus sit externi & publici sacrificii, quàm sacrificium Missæ. Respond. Λειτυργία Græcis propriè designat munus publicum profanum, quasi λαϊτουργία, a λαΐτον ἔργον, ut explicat Suidas: quo sensu λειτουργὸς dicitur magistratus Rom.13,4. Synecdochicè declarat munus publicum sacrum, in prædicando Evangelio, & celebrandis sacramentis & precibus. Unde λειτουργούντων diserte explicat Chrysostomus per χηρυττόντων, hoc est, prædicantibus, & Syrus per מתכשפין metha-schephin, hoc est, precantibus, innuens ministerium sacrum universum; cujus precatio est pars. Et Chrysostomum sequitur Erasmus; qui de prædicatione Evangelii itidem exponit: ut ut hodierni Græci & Syri, perinde ac Latini, hac voce abutantur.
units.tr: Second, the passage Acts 13:2, where the Apostles are said to be ministering [λειτουργοῦντες, leitourgountes]. Here Bellarmine asserts that leitourgia signifies sacrifice, and that today among the Greeks it is the same as what the Mass is among the Latins; and among the Syrians it is methcaschphanuta. From this he gathers that the Apostles too once sacrificed, that is, offered Christ in the holy Supper, since there is no kind of external and public sacrifice other than the sacrifice of the Mass. Answer: among the Greeks leitourgia properly denotes a public, secular office, as if from laitourgia, from laiton ergon [λαΐτον ἔργον], as Suidas explains. In this sense the magistrate is called leitourgos (Rom. 13:4). By synecdoche it denotes a public sacred office, in preaching the Gospel, celebrating the sacraments, and offering prayers. Hence Chrysostom expressly explains leitourgounton as preaching [κηρυττόντων], that is, preaching, and the Syrian explains it as metha-schephin, that is, praying, implying the whole sacred ministry, of which prayer is only a part. Erasmus follows Chrysostom and likewise explains it of the preaching of the Gospel, although today's Greeks and Syrians, just like the Latins, abuse this word.

units.la: XXVI.
units.tr: XXVI.

units.la: Tertiò, Locus 1.Cor.10,14, 15. ubi mensa Domini conseritur non modò cum mensis gentilium & Iudæorum; quæ vera erant altaria, sed etiam cum veris eorundem sacrificiis: item societas; quam cum Christo habemus ex manducatione Eucharistiæ, cum societate illorum; quam cum suis sacrificiis ipsi habebant ex manducatione idolothytorum. Unde colligit ille, in nostra quoque Eucharistia verum & reale sacrificium offerri, &c.
units.tr: Thirdly, there is the passage at 1 Corinthians 10:14-15, where the Lord's table is compared not only with the tables of the Gentiles and Jews, which were true altars, but also with their real sacrifices. Likewise, the fellowship we have with Christ through eating the Eucharist is compared with the fellowship they themselves had through eating the idol-offerings in their sacrifices. From this he concludes that a true and real sacrifice is also offered in our Eucharist, etc.

units.la: Respond. Concedi potest in Eucharistia sacrificium esse, si modò res ipsa rectè explicetur: sed sacrificium non externum & proprium; in quo Christi corpus et sanguis offerantur substantialiter & reipsa, sed mysticum: sicut ibi Paulus ipse explicat, Poculum benedictionis; cui benedicimus, nonne communio sanguinis Christi est? Panis; quem frangimus nonne communio corporis Christi est? Sophisma igitur secundùm quid implicatur: quum Apostolus significationem Eucharistiæ mysticam tantùm urgeat, eóq; finem & usum illius per exempla similia, quæ tamen κατά τι semper sunt accipienda, illustret.
units.tr: Answer: It may be conceded that there is a sacrifice in the Eucharist, provided the matter is rightly explained. But it is not an external and proper sacrifice, in which the body and blood of Christ are offered substantially and in very fact. It is a mystical sacrifice. Paul himself explains this there: "The cup of blessing which we bless, is it not the communion of the blood of Christ? The bread which we break, is it not the communion of the body of Christ?" The sophism is therefore a fallacy of qualified sense. The Apostle is pressing only the mystical signification of the Eucharist, and by similar examples he illustrates its end and use. These examples, however, must always be taken in a certain respect [κατά τι].

units.la: XXVII.
units.tr: XXVII.

units.la: Quoad PATRVM dicta; in quibus Eucharistiam vocant sacrificium, oblationem, immolationem, hostiam, victimam, &c. sciendum, illos non sensisse, quasi corpus Christi immoletur iterum: sed voluerunt, fidelibus in sacro illo convivio Christum cum suis beneficiis exhiberi, & recoli memoriam sacrificii ejus facti in cruce, &c. Atq; sic Eusebius explicat, quum inquit: Θυόμεν, καὶ θυμιῶμεν τότε μὲν τὴν μνήμην τῆς μεγάλης θυμάτων, κατὰ τὰ πρὸς αὐτῆς παραδοθέντα μυστήρια ὅπιτε. βαλλεῦντες, καὶ τὴν ὑπὲρ σωτηρίας ἡμῶν εὐχαριστίαν, λέγ ἰυσιῶν ὕμνων, καὶ εὐχῶν τῷ Θεῷ προσνομίζοντες, &c. Et Augustinus : Hujus sacrificii caro & sanguis ante adventum Christi per victimarum similitudinem promittebatur: in passione Christi per ipsam veritatem reddebatur : post ascensum Christi per sacramentum memoriae celebratur, &c. Et Chrysostomus Eucharistiam vocat προσφορὰν ἀναμνηκὴν : & Iustinus Martyr εὐχαριστικὴν λογολογίαν, &c. Neque hic elabitur Iesuita distinctione sacrificii cruenti & incruenti. Nam de incruento sacrificio scriptura nihil novit : nec sine sanguine fit ulla remissio aut expiatio. Alioqui oportuisset Christum saepe passum esse, quod est ἀδύνατον, inquit Apostolus Heb.9, 26. quia oblationem suimet ipsius unicâ morte suâ peregit : seu, quia Christi oblatio in ejus cruento sacrificio mortis, in cruce peracto, consistit. Incruentum ergo in Ecclesia Christiana sacrificium non retinetur, nisi quia Ecclesia annuntiat mortem & resurrectionem unigeniti filii Dei, ait Concilium Ephesinum.
units.tr: As for the sayings of the Fathers, in which they call the Eucharist a sacrifice, an oblation, an immolation, a victim, a host, and so on, it should be known that they did not mean that the body of Christ is sacrificed again. They wanted Christ, with his benefits, to be set forth to the faithful in that sacred banquet, and the memory of the sacrifice made on the cross to be recalled, etc. So Eusebius explains when he says: "We sacrifice and offer incense, then indeed the memory of the great sacrifice, according to the mysteries handed down by him [...] throwing, and the thanksgiving for our salvation, offering hymns and prayers to God, etc." [Greek]. And Augustine: "The flesh and blood of this sacrifice were promised before the coming of Christ through the likeness of victims; in the passion of Christ they were rendered through the truth itself; after the ascension of Christ they are celebrated through the sacrament of memorial," etc. Chrysostom calls the Eucharist a remembrance offering [προσφορὰν ἀναμνηκὴν], and Justin Martyr calls it a eucharistic discourse [εὐχαριστικὴν λογολογίαν], etc. Nor does the Jesuit escape here by his distinction between bloody and unbloody sacrifice. For Scripture knows nothing of an unbloody sacrifice, and no remission or expiation takes place without blood. Otherwise Christ would have had to suffer often, which is "impossible," as the Apostle says, Heb. 9:26, since he accomplished the offering of himself by his one death; or, because Christ's offering consists in the death of his bloody sacrifice, accomplished on the cross. Therefore an unbloody sacrifice is not retained in the Christian Church, except in that the Church proclaims the death and resurrection of the only-begotten Son of God, as the Council of Ephesus says.

units.la: XXVIII.
units.tr: XXVIII.

units.la: Sed his argumentis Bellarminus evincere nititur, Missam esse sacrificium externum, proprie dictum. Videamus paucis ea, quibus eam vult esse sacrificium propitiatorium.
units.tr: But Bellarmine strives to prove by these arguments that the Mass is an external sacrifice, properly so called. Let us briefly examine those by which he wants it to be a propitiatory sacrifice.

units.la: 1. Argumentum primum : Sacrificia vet. Test. fuerunt propitiatoria, ut ex Levitico et Iobi historia constat, ubi Iob sacrificavit pro peccatis filiorum suorum, &c. Ergo etiam hodie Missa sacrificium propitiatorium statui potest.
units.tr: 1. First argument: The sacrifices of the Old Testament were propitiatory, as is clear from Leviticus and from the history of Job, where Job sacrificed for the sins of his sons, etc. Therefore the Mass can also today be established as a propitiatory sacrifice.

units.la: Respond. Sacrificia quaedam V. T. vocantur propitiatoria non proprie ; quia sanguis taurorum & hircorum peccata auferre nequit, Heb. 10, 4. sed improprie & figurate, ratione nimirum typi & significati, quia adumbrabant & significabant sacrificium unicum expiatorium, quod oblaturus erat pro peccatis nostris Christus, pontifex magnus, in cruce Heb.10,10. Vocantur etiam propitiatoria propter similitudinem : quia in externa conversatione merebantur peccatorum remissionem, id est, reconciliabant eos ; qui peccaverant, ne excluderentur ab Ecclesia.
units.tr: Answer: Certain sacrifices of the Old Testament are called propitiatory not properly, because the blood of bulls and goats cannot take away sins (Heb. 10:4), but improperly and figuratively, namely by reason of the type and the thing signified. They foreshadowed and signified the one expiatory sacrifice which Christ, the great high priest, was to offer for our sins on the cross (Heb. 10:10). They are also called propitiatory on account of resemblance: because in outward fellowship they merited the remission of sins, that is, they reconciled those who had sinned, so that they would not be excluded from the Church.

units.la: 2. Argumentum secundum : In sacra Coena fuit sanguis Christi effusus pro multis in remissionem peccatorum. Idem vero jam fit in Missa. Ergo in hac fit sacrificium propitiatorium. Respond. Supra ostensum est, Christum in sacra Cæna vere & realiter seipsum non sacrificâsse, sed sacramentum & memoriam instituisse sacrificii sui, quod erat postero die facturus in cruce. Alioquin si sacrificium, quod Christus in sacra Cæna debuit obtulisse, idem fuit cum eo, quod obtulit in cruce, tum super vacaneum illi fuit postero die mori: quia jam ante redemtio fuisset perfecta, quod est absurdum simul & blasphemum.
units.tr: 2. Second argument: In the Lord's Supper Christ's blood was poured out for many for the remission of sins. But the same now happens in the Mass. Therefore a propitiatory sacrifice is made in it. Answer: It has been shown above that Christ in the Lord's Supper did not truly and really sacrifice himself. Rather, he instituted a sacrament and a memorial of his sacrifice, which he was to make the next day on the cross. Otherwise, if the sacrifice which Christ was to have offered at the Supper was the same as the one he offered on the cross, it would have been superfluous for him to die the next day, since redemption would already have been completed. That is absurd and at the same time blasphemous.

units.la: 3. Argumentum tertium: Omnis pontifex ex hominibus assumtus pro hominibus constituitur, in his, quæ sunt ad Deum, ut offerat dona, & sacrificia pro peccatis, &c. Hic si cujusvis sacerdotis est offerre dona & sacrificia pro peccatis: Ergo erit etiam sacerdotis novi Testamenti.
units.tr: 3. Third argument: Every high priest taken from among men is appointed for men in the things pertaining to God, that he may offer gifts and sacrifices for sins, etc. If it is the office of any priest to offer gifts and sacrifices for sins, then it will also be the office of a priest of the New Testament.

units.la: ● Respond. Loquitur Apostolus non generatim de omnibus ministris verbi, sed de omnibus sacerdotibus legalibus, atque imprimis de pontifice magno; qui figura fuit Christi: quam figuram postea in sacerdotio & sacrificio Christi propitiatorio impletam esse docet cap.7.9.&10.
units.tr: Answer: The Apostle speaks not generally of all ministers of the Word, but of all legal priests, and above all of the high priest, who was a figure of Christ. This figure he teaches was afterwards fulfilled in the priesthood and propitiatory sacrifice of Christ, in chapters 7, 9 and 10.

units.la: XXIX.
units.tr: XXIX.

units.la: Hæc præcipua sunt argumenta Bellarmini, quibus Missam stabilire nititur, & eorum ἀναστκδὴν. Cætera, quæ ad accurationem tum ἀναστκδὴν, tum κατασκευὴν totius hujusce tractationis pertinent, videre licet apud Illustrem Dn. Plæsseum Mornæum, & clariss. Dn. Hospinianum nostrum; quos honoris caussâ nomino. Quod restat, verum & æternum sacerdotem, DN. IESVM, toto pectore oro, ut veritatem suam contra humanæ rationis sophismata in animis electorum suorum stabilire velit. Eidem sit gloria in sempiterna secula, Amen.
units.tr: These are the chief arguments of Bellarmine, by which he strives to establish the Mass, together with their refutation [ἀνασκευήν]. The rest, which pertain to the accuracy both of the refutation [ἀνασκευήν] and of the construction [κατασκευήν] of this whole treatment, may be seen in the Illustrious Lord Du Plessis Mornay and in our distinguished Lord Hospinian, whom I name out of respect. As for what remains, I pray with my whole heart to the true and eternal priest, our Lord Jesus, that he may be pleased to establish his truth in the minds of his elect against the sophisms of human reason. To him be glory for ever and ever, Amen.

units.tr: THE END
